name: Tibia
func: The shinbone, the main weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. It carries body weight from the knee down to the ankle and anchors key muscles and ligaments.

levels.kid:
Run your hand down the front of your leg below your knee. That hard edge is your **shinbone**, called the **tibia**.

It is the big, strong bone in your lower leg. It holds up almost all of your weight when you stand, walk and jump. At the top it makes part of your **knee**, and at the bottom it makes part of your **ankle**.

There is hardly any muscle or fat over the front of it, which is why bumping your shin hurts so much! A thinner bone called the fibula sits right next to it on the outside.
levels.hs:
The **tibia** is the larger, medial bone of the leg (the part between knee and ankle) and the second-longest bone in the body after the femur. It sits on the inner (big-toe) side, with the slender **fibula** beside it laterally, joined to it along its length by the **interosseous membrane**.

Its wide top, the **tibial plateau**, has a **medial** and a **lateral condyle** that support the femur at the knee. The **menisci** (C-shaped cartilage pads) sit on top of the plateau, and the **cruciate ligaments** attach to the bumpy area between the condyles. Just below the front of the knee is the **tibial tuberosity**, where the patellar ligament attaches.

The shaft is triangular in cross-section. Its sharp **anterior border** (the shin) and flat **medial surface** lie right under the skin. At the ankle, the tibia ends in the **medial malleolus**, the bump on the inside of your ankle, and its lower surface sits on the **talus** to form the ankle joint.

The tibia carries most of the body's weight through the leg, roughly 80–90% by common estimates, with the fibula carrying the rest.
levels.college:
**Proximal tibia:** the medial condyle is larger and oval with a concave articular surface; the lateral condyle is smaller and nearly flat to slightly convex. Between them lies the **intercondylar eminence** with medial and lateral tubercles; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas give attachment to the ACL, PCL and meniscal horns. The lateral condyle carries a facet underneath for the **proximal tibiofibular joint**. **Gerdy's tubercle**, on the anterolateral condyle, is the insertion of the **iliotibial band**.

**Shaft:** three borders (anterior, medial, interosseous) and three surfaces (medial, lateral, posterior). The lateral surface is covered by tibialis anterior. The posterior surface shows the **soleal line**, where soleus arises, with popliteus above it and tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus below. The **pes anserinus** (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) inserts on the upper medial surface.

**Distal tibia:** the inferior articular surface (the **plafond**) and the medial malleolus form most of the **ankle mortise** with the lateral malleolus of the fibula. A groove behind the medial malleolus carries the tibialis posterior tendon. The **distal tibiofibular syndesmosis** joins the two bones just above the joint.

**Neighbours:** the anterior tibial artery and deep fibular nerve run in front of the interosseous membrane; the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve run behind the bone in the deep posterior compartment. The **great saphenous vein** passes in front of the medial malleolus.

The tibia's nutrient artery, one of the largest in the body, enters posteriorly near the soleal line.
levels.phd:
The tibia ossifies from a **primary centre** in the shaft (appearing around the seventh fetal week) and secondary centres in the proximal and distal ends. The proximal epiphysis, whose centre is usually present at birth, extends a tongue anteriorly to form the tuberosity; this apophysis is under heavy traction from the quadriceps during adolescent growth spurts. Most longitudinal growth of the tibia occurs at the **proximal physis**.

Its shape reflects loading. Diaphyseal cortical bone is thickest where bending stresses are highest; long-term loading changes the cross-sectional geometry, as athletes' tibiae show greater cortical area and polar moment of inertia than non-athletes' (pQCT studies of runners and jumpers). This is **Wolff's law** in action, mediated by **osteocytes** sensing fluid shear in their lacunar–canalicular network and signalling through **sclerostin** and the **RANKL/OPG** balance.

Blood supply is clinically decisive. The diaphysis receives a single **nutrient artery** from the posterior tibial artery, supplying the inner two-thirds of the cortex, while the outer third depends on **periosteal vessels**. The anteromedial surface has almost no muscle cover, so periosteal supply there is thin. When high-energy trauma strips periosteum and disrupts the nutrient artery, healing slows, which is a major reason tibial shaft fractures have among the highest rates of **delayed union and nonunion** of any long bone.

**Tibial torsion** (external rotation of the distal tibia relative to the proximal) increases during childhood, reaching roughly 15–20° in adults, though values vary between studies and measurement methods.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** the subcutaneous anteromedial surface makes deformity, open wounds and tenderness easy to detect. Assess the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, and sensation in the first web space (deep fibular nerve) and sole (tibial nerve).

**Tibial shaft fractures** are the most common long-bone fracture and frequently **open**, because so little soft tissue covers the bone. Open fractures are graded with the **Gustilo–Anderson** classification and need urgent antibiotics, debridement and stabilisation. Definitive treatment is commonly an **intramedullary nail**; plates or external fixators are used depending on location and soft-tissue state.

**Compartment syndrome** is the feared complication: rising pressure within the leg's fascial compartments chokes perfusion. The classic early sign is **pain out of proportion**, worsened by passive stretch of the compartment's muscles; pulses are often still present. Treatment is emergency **fasciotomy** of all four compartments.

**Tibial plateau fractures** (Schatzker classification) usually involve the lateral plateau and need CT for planning. **Pilon fractures** drive the talus into the plafond.

In teenagers: **Osgood–Schlatter disease** (painful tuberosity from traction apophysitis), and **tibial stress fractures** in runners, which may be invisible on early X-rays but show on MRI as marrow oedema. A **toddler's fracture** is a subtle spiral shaft fracture in young children.

The tibia is also a surgical resource: the proximal tibia and intramedullary canal are used for bone graft harvest, and in emergencies the proximal tibia is a standard **intraosseous access** site when veins cannot be found.

keyPoints: Medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg
Tibial plateau supports the femur; tuberosity takes the patellar ligament
Medial malleolus forms the inner ankle
Thin soft-tissue cover: fractures are often open and heal slowly
Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch

test.q: Which bump on the tibia is the attachment of the patellar ligament?
test.explain: The patellar ligament inserts on the tibial tuberosity; Gerdy's tubercle takes the iliotibial band.

test.q: The bump on the inner side of the ankle is the medial ______ of the tibia.
test.explain: The medial malleolus is part of the tibia; the lateral malleolus belongs to the fibula.

test.q: Why do tibial shaft fractures so often become open fractures?
choices: The anteromedial surface lies just under the skin
test.explain: With almost no muscle over the front, broken ends easily pierce the skin.

test.q: What is the classic early sign of compartment syndrome?
choices: Pain out of proportion, worse with passive stretch
test.explain: Pulses are often still present early; pain on passive stretch is the key warning.

test.q: Painful traction irritation of the tibial tuberosity in active teenagers is called ______ disease.
test.explain: Repeated quadriceps pull on the growing tuberosity apophysis causes pain and a bony lump.
